intro: To force quit Canva on Mac, press Option, Command and Esc together, select Canva in the Force Quit window, and click Force Quit. Try Command-Q first, because a normal quit lets Canva finish saving, and save any work you can before you force it.
tldr: Click the Canva window, then press Command-Q. A normal quit lets Canva finish saving.
If Canva is stuck, press Option-Command-Esc, select Canva, and click Force Quit.
The Dock also works: Control-click the Canva icon and choose Force Quit.
If Force Quit does nothing, use Activity Monitor. Restart the Mac only as a last resort.
Force quitting can lose unsaved changes, so check your design after Canva reopens.

blocks.text: A frozen Canva window is annoying, mostly because you cannot tell whether your work is safe. Usually the app is busy, or it has stopped answering clicks. macOS gives you a way to close it from outside the window, and that is what people mean by force quitting. The steps below go from the gentlest method to the strongest one, so you only reach for the heavy tools when you need them.
Pick the right way to force quit Canva

Work down the table in order. Each method is a little stronger than the one before it, and each one carries more risk to unsaved work. Most freezes end at the first or second method. You only need Activity Monitor or a restart in rare cases. If you are unsure, start with Command-Q and wait a few seconds.

blocks.caption: Choose the gentlest method that fits what Canva is doing.

blocks.text: Try a normal quit before you force quit Canva

Start with Command-Q. Click inside the Canva window first, so Canva is the active app, then press Command and Q together. A normal quit lets the app finish saving, according to Mole's guide to force quitting. Give it a few seconds. If the window does not close, the app may be stuck, and that is when a force quit makes sense.
A common mistake is to hold Command-Q down or press it again and again. That does not speed anything up. It also leaves you unsure whether the first press worked. Press it once, then wait.

If Canva is busy with a long task, a quit can take longer than you expect. Watch the screen for a short while. A spinning cursor that clears or a window that begins to fade is a sign the quit is moving.
Use the Force Quit window and its shortcut

The Force Quit window is the standard macOS tool for an app that will not respond. Press Option, Command and Esc together to open it. You can also click the Apple logo in the top-left corner and choose Force Quit. Apple's support page lists both routes.

Once the window is open, select Canva and click Force Quit. The app closes at once. Apple warns that you may lose unsaved changes, so treat this step as the last chance to save anything you have not saved.

The shortcut is quicker when your keyboard still responds. The Apple menu suits people who prefer the mouse or trackpad. On a Mac with a Touch Bar, the Esc key sits on the left side of the bar, which trips up some people the first time.
Force quit Canva from the Dock

The Dock route is useful when the Force Quit window will not open. Control-click the Canva icon, then pick Force Quit from the menu. This only works while Canva is running. Some guides also say right-click works. Mole's test used Control-click, so start with that.

The same warning about unsaved changes applies here. Once Canva is back on screen, check your design before you keep working. If the Dock menu has no Force Quit option, Canva may already be closed, and you can open it again from the Dock.
Use Activity Monitor when Force Quit does nothing

Activity Monitor shows every process running on your Mac. That makes it the best place to check whether Canva is stuck or just slow. Open it from Applications > Utilities, then type Canva in the search box in the top-right corner of the window.

Select the Canva process, then click the stop button in the toolbar, the octagon with an X. In the dialog, choose Quit first. Choose Force Quit only if Quit does nothing. Quit asks the process to close itself, which gives it a chance to save. Force Quit stops it straight away.
What Not Responding means in Activity Monitor

Mole's guide says Activity Monitor marks unresponsive processes as (Not Responding) in red. That label means the process has stopped answering. It does not mean your design is gone. It also does not tell you how far the last save got.

If Canva shows up more than once, work with the entry marked (Not Responding) and leave the others alone. Quitting a process that is still working can cost you edits it has not saved yet. Treat the label as your guide, not the name alone.
A worked example: Canva freezes during a resize
Here is a typical sequence, written as an example and not as a report of a known Canva bug. You are resizing a design and dragging a corner. The cursor stops moving, and Canva ignores the next click.

First, you wait a few seconds. Then you press Command-Q, and nothing happens. Next, you press Option, Command and Esc, select Canva, and click Force Quit. The app closes, and the Mac keeps running normally.

When you open Canva again, check the design. The resize may have stuck, or it may need redoing. Redo it, then export a copy before you move on. The resize steps are at /how-to/resize-a-design-in-canva.
Restart the Mac as a last resort
A restart closes every app and any stuck process at once. Use it when Canva keeps freezing after the other methods, or when the whole Mac stops responding. Choose Apple menu > Restart first.

If the Mac will not restart, Apple's guide says to press and hold the power button for up to 10 seconds until it turns off. On Macs with Touch ID, hold the Touch ID button instead. A forced power-off skips the normal shutdown, so open work in other apps can be lost too. Save what you can first, if you still can.
What to check after Canva reopens

Open the design before you do anything else. Check that your last edit is still there. Scroll to the page you were working on, and look at any text or images you moved. A force quit can drop changes that had not been saved yet.

It is quicker to redo one move now than to find a gap after you export. If a design has gone missing completely, the restore guide explains how deleted designs come back: /how-to/restore-a-deleted-design-in-canva.
Back up a design before risky work

A force quit only hurts when there is work to lose. The cheapest protection is a copy. Before a big resize, a batch of edits, or a long export, duplicate the design. The duplicate gives you a fallback if the original freezes in a bad state. The steps are in /how-to/duplicate-a-design-in-canva.

For a snapshot you can open anywhere, download a PDF as well. Keep the PDF in a folder outside Canva, so you can still check the work when the app will not open. The download steps are in /how-to/download-a-design-as-pdf-in-canva. Neither step replaces saving. They give you something to fall back on.
Mistakes people make when Canva freezes

items: Force quitting on the first freeze. Give the app a moment, and try Command-Q first.
Clicking Force Quit more than once. One click is enough, and the window needs a moment to close.
Restarting the Mac before checking Activity Monitor. A restart works, but it also closes every other app.
Reinstalling Canva as the first fix. Try a restart and an update before you remove the app.
Skipping the check after reopening. The last edit before a freeze is the one to check first.

blocks.text: Check your Canva version before you update

Canva's download page does not show a version number, so the site alone will not tell you which build is current. A Mole test dated September 19, 2026 lists version 1.125.1 from the official download. The same test lists 1.126.0 as the version the app updated itself to while installed.

If your copy is older than those, update it. Canva's release notes were not reachable for this guide, so those two numbers are the best reference here. The install and update steps are in the install guide: /how-to/download-and-install-canva-in-canva.
Canva in a browser is a different case

This guide covers the Canva desktop app. If you use Canva in Chrome or Safari, the Force Quit window lists the browser as an app, so you can force quit it the same way. Closing the Canva tab is often the simplest move first.
Canva's own help pages did not load for this guide, so the Canva-specific steps here come from a third-party test. Apple's steps cover every Mac app, so they are the firmest part of this page.
Keep Canva from freezing again

Keep the app updated, and restart the Mac now and then so stuck processes do not pile up. If Canva keeps freezing, try the desktop app reset guide at /how-to/reset-the-desktop-app-in-canva. That guide covers the reset steps in more detail.

The Mole test also notes that a Canva login item can stay listed even after the app is removed. If Canva opens by itself after a restart, check System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions. For faster work once Canva is running again, the shortcuts guide is at /how-to/use-keyboard-shortcuts-in-canva.

faq.question: Will force quitting Canva delete my design?
faq.answer: Usually not. A force quit ends the app right away, and Apple warns that unsaved changes can be lost. Mole's Canva test reports that Canva also warns about this. Open the design once Canva reopens and check your last edits.

faq.question: What is the Force Quit shortcut on a Mac?
faq.answer: It is Option, Command and Esc pressed together, written ⌥⌘Esc. It opens the Force Quit window. You still select Canva and click Force Quit to close it.

faq.question: Does Command-Q work when Canva is frozen?
faq.answer: Sometimes. A frozen app may ignore it, so give it a few seconds, then move to the Force Quit window. Mole's guide suggests Command-Q first because it lets the app finish saving.

faq.question: Can I force quit Canva without the keyboard?
faq.answer: Yes. Control-click the Canva icon in the Dock and choose Force Quit, or click the Apple logo and choose Force Quit. Both routes work with a mouse or trackpad.

faq.question: What does Not Responding mean in Activity Monitor?
faq.answer: It means the process has stopped answering. Mole's guide says Activity Monitor marks it in red as (Not Responding). Choose Quit first, and use Force Quit only if Quit does nothing.

faq.question: Do I need the latest version of Canva to stop freezing?
faq.answer: Not always, but an older build is a reasonable thing to rule out first. Mole's September 2026 test lists 1.125.1 and 1.126.0. Canva's download page does not show a version number, so compare your copy with those.

faq.question: Does this guide cover Canva in a web browser?
faq.answer: No. It covers the desktop app. For a browser tab, close the tab first. Canva's web-specific steps could not be checked for this guide.

steps.name: Try a normal quit with Command-Q
steps.text: Click anywhere in the Canva window so it is the active app, then press Command and Q together. Give it a few seconds to close on its own.
steps.tip: If the window does not close after a few seconds, move on to the Force Quit window.

steps.name: Open the Force Quit window
steps.text: Press Option, Command and Esc together. You can also click the Apple logo in the top-left corner and choose Force Quit.
steps.tip: On Macs with a Touch Bar, the Esc key is on the left side of the bar.

steps.name: Select Canva in the app list
steps.text: Find Canva in the list of open apps and click it once so it is highlighted. If Canva is not listed, it may already be closed, so open it from the Dock and check.

steps.name: Click Force Quit
steps.text: Click Force Quit. Canva closes right away, and unsaved changes can be lost.
steps.tip: One click is enough. Give the window a moment before you click again.

steps.name: Force quit Canva from the Dock
steps.text: If the Force Quit window will not open, use the Dock. Control-click the Canva icon, then choose Force Quit from the menu. Canva must be running for this to work.
steps.tip: Some guides say right-click works too. Control-click is the method Mole tested.

steps.name: Find Canva in Activity Monitor
steps.text: Open Activity Monitor from Applications > Utilities. Type Canva in the search box in the top-right corner.
steps.tip: A stuck process is marked (Not Responding) in red. Look for that label.

steps.name: Quit the stuck process, then force it
steps.text: Select the Canva process, then click the stop button in the toolbar, the octagon with an X. In the dialog, choose Quit first. Choose Force Quit only if Quit does nothing.
steps.tip: Quit asks the process to close itself. Force Quit stops it immediately.

steps.name: Restart the Mac if Canva is still stuck
steps.text: Choose Apple menu > Restart. If the whole Mac stops responding, press and hold the power button for up to 10 seconds until it turns off. On Macs with Touch ID, hold the Touch ID button instead.
steps.tip: Use the power button only when a normal restart is not possible.

steps.name: Reopen Canva and check your work
steps.text: Open Canva from the Dock or the Applications folder, then reopen the design you were editing. Check that your last changes are there before you keep working.
steps.tip: If a design is missing, the restore guide covers deleted designs.

shortcuts.action: Force quit Canva from the Dock

troubleshooting.problem: Canva is not in the Force Quit list
troubleshooting.fix: It may already be closed. Open Activity Monitor and search for Canva to see whether any Canva process is still running.

troubleshooting.problem: Force Quit does nothing at all
troubleshooting.fix: Use Activity Monitor and choose Force Quit in the dialog if Quit does nothing. If the whole Mac is frozen, restart from the Apple menu, or hold the power button for up to 10 seconds.

troubleshooting.problem: Canva opens again by itself after a restart
troubleshooting.fix: Check System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions and turn off any Canva item you do not want opening at login.

troubleshooting.problem: Your last edit is missing after reopening
troubleshooting.fix: That edit probably was not saved before the freeze. Redo the change, then close the design with Command-Q next time.
Update the app, then try the desktop app reset guide. Reinstalling is the last step, not the first.
